case_study_insert.main_stem: Mendip Gasket & Fasteners (MGF) is a private limited company in the industrial components sector, employing a workforce of 60. Founded in 2011 by Priya Mendip, it supplies precision gaskets and fasteners to commercial vehicle assemblers and operates a hierarchical structure with autocratic leadership. MGF plans to invest $720,000 in a new CNC machining cell, financed by a $450,000 ten-year bank loan and $270,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $300,000 a year, a variable cost of $8.00 a unit and a selling price of $14.00, and produces 75,000 units a year. MGF faces two operational problems: the defect rate on machined seals has reached 2.4% and labour turnover is rising among skilled machinists.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Operations and Quality Report — Q4 2025: The gasket line machined 18,750 units last quarter at a defect rate of 2.4%, up from 1.6% a year earlier. Customer returns rose from 14 to 31 per month. Average delivery lead time is 6.5 days, against a promised 5 days. A survey of 400 commercial vehicle buyers found that 58% rank dimensional accuracy as the main purchase criterion and 47% would switch supplier after two late deliveries. Time-and-attendance records show 11 of 60 skilled machinists took more than 10 days of unplanned leave last quarter; replacement agency cover costs $280 a day.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Mendip Gasket & Fasteners as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (January 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.50% to 5.25%, increasing borrowing costs for firms with variable-rate loans. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 7.2% from $12.50 to $13.40 per hour from April 2026, raising wage bills across engineering firms. (3) Wholesale steel and alloy prices have risen 9.0% year-on-year, while industrial input-cost inflation stands at 6.3% and demand from commercial vehicle assemblers is forecast to grow 2.8%.

questions.question_text: MGF plans to fund part of its $720,000 CNC machining cell from retained profit. Explain two advantages for MGF of using retained profit rather than increasing its $450,000 bank loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Retained profit carries no interest charge and no compulsory repayment. MGF must already meet fixed costs of $300,000 a year and service a $450,000 ten-year bank loan, so funding $270,000 of the $720,000 CNC cell internally avoids adding another fixed interest commitment. With the base rate raised to 5.25%, any further variable-rate borrowing would increase costs again, whereas retained profit leaves cash flow free to absorb the rework caused by the 2.4% defect rate on machined seals.

Point 2: Using $270,000 of retained profit keeps control with founder Priya Mendip and avoids the collateral and lender conditions attached to more debt. Because MGF is already committed to a $450,000 loan, a smaller debt burden reduces the risk that a fall in orders from commercial vehicle assemblers leaves the firm unable to meet repayments. Internal funding also shows that the business can support part of its own expansion, which strengthens its position if it seeks finance later.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid point identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual explanation and analysis applied to MGF.

questions.question_text: MGF is launching a new alloy fastener range. Consider trade press advertising, an industry exhibition, or direct sales visits to assemblers. Which should MGF choose to win new contracts? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Trade press advertising: A campaign in a commercial-vehicle engineering magazine would reach assemblers' technical managers nationally at a low cost per reader. However, print cannot demonstrate the dimensional accuracy that 58% of the 400 surveyed buyers rank as the main purchase criterion, and it does nothing to answer concerns about the 6.5-day delivery lead time against a 5-day promise. For a business carrying $300,000 of fixed costs, spending that does not prove tolerances is difficult to justify.

Industry exhibition: A stand would let MGF show machined samples and meet several assemblers in one place, giving technical credibility. Yet stand fees, travel and staff time are expensive, and results depend on who visits. With a workforce of 60, the machinists manning the stand would be away from the CNC cell while the defect rate is already 2.4%, so output of 75,000 units could suffer.

Direct sales visits: An engineer can visit procurement teams with test certificates, answer questions on accuracy and negotiate delivery personally. This directly addresses the 47% of surveyed buyers who would switch supplier after two late deliveries, because MGF can explain how it will shorten the 6.5-day lead time. The cost per contract is higher in travel time, but each buyer approached is already qualified, so conversion is more likely than with print.

Recommendation: MGF should choose direct sales visits. They convert the 58% who buy on accuracy and reassure the 47% at risk from late delivery, which neither print advertising nor a passive exhibition stand achieves as reliably. Trade press is rejected as too indirect and unable to prove tolerances; the exhibition is rejected because its high fixed cost and staffing demands pull scarce machinists away from the $720,000 CNC cell. MGF should follow up visits with brief emails containing dimensional data.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited description of the three promotional routes with little reference to MGF's buyers.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Discussion of at least two routes with applied reference to MGF's survey, lead time and costs and some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three routes applied to MGF, with a clear recommendation explaining why trade press and the exhibition are rejected.

questions.question_text: MGF's defect rate on machined seals has reached 2.4% and labour turnover is rising. Explain two benefits for MGF of using democratic leadership instead of its current autocratic style.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Democratic leadership gives MGF's 60 employees a voice in how the new CNC machining cell is organised, tackling the rising labour turnover among skilled machinists. Under the current autocratic style, decisions come from Priya Mendip alone, so the machinists who handle the seals daily have no route to flag problems. Involving them in setting tolerances raises ownership and job satisfaction, which should reduce the 11 of 60 workers who took more than ten days of unplanned leave.

Point 2: Consultation produces practical suggestions that an autocratic manager may miss. Machinists closest to the 2.4% defect rate can propose fixture or cutting-speed changes, improving quality without further capital beyond the $720,000 cell. Fewer defects mean less rework and less demand for agency cover at $280 a day, protecting the $300,000 fixed-cost base. Democratic leadership also helps retain the skilled staff needed to operate the cell once the $450,000 loan repayments begin.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid point identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual explanation and analysis applied to MGF.

questions.question_text: MGF wants to reduce the 2.4% defect rate and the absence among 11 of 60 machinists. Consider a productivity bonus or team working. Which should MGF choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
Productivity bonus: Paying machinists for output above a target would raise effort and could spread the $300,000 fixed costs over more of the 75,000 units. It is easy to understand and links pay to results. However, a volume-based bonus rewards speed at precisely the wrong time: the defect rate on machined seals is already 2.4%, and 58% of surveyed buyers rank dimensional accuracy first, so faster working could create more rejected parts and more returns, undoing the benefit of extra output.

Team working: Organising machinists into small teams responsible for a whole batch means members check one another's work, so defects are caught before parts leave the cell. Teams can rotate tasks, reducing the boredom behind 11 of 60 workers taking more than ten days of unplanned leave, and peer support eases the pressure that drives labour turnover. This uses the skilled staff MGF already employs, avoiding further agency cover at $280 a day while the $720,000 cell beds in. The weaknesses are that group norms can shield slow members and that targets must be explicit.

Decision: MGF should choose team working. It attacks both problems at source — the 2.4% defect rate and the absence among 11 of 60 machinists — while a productivity bonus risks trading quality for volume when 58% of customers buy on accuracy and 47% would change supplier after late deliveries. A bonus could be added only after the defect rate falls; it should not be introduced now. Across 75,000 units a year, fewer rejected parts protect the $14.00 selling price and the cash available to meet the $300,000 fixed costs.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of a bonus and team working with little application to MGF.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of one or both methods using MGF's defect, absence and agency-cover data.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Full evaluation of both methods applied to MGF with a justified decision and clear rejection of the productivity bonus.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how MGF's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.
questions.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $300,000 ÷ ($14.00 − $8.00) = $300,000 ÷ $6.00 = 50,000 units. | Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $14.00 − $8.00 = $6.00. | (iii) Four contextual uses explained.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $300,000 ÷ ($14.00 − $8.00) = $300,000 ÷ $6.00 = 50,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 50,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $14.00 − $8.00 = $6.00. Answer: contribution per unit is $6.00.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways MGF's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. MGF can compare the 50,000-unit break-even output with actual output of 75,000 units, giving a margin of safety of 25,000 units, to decide whether to run the new CNC cell at full capacity.
2. Contribution of $6.00 lets managers test a price discount for assemblers: cutting the $14.00 price by $0.50 leaves $5.50 contribution, so the $300,000 fixed costs require 54,546 units, a volume check before discounting.
3. With fixed costs of $300,000 and 50,000 units needed to break even, managers can judge whether the $450,000 loan can be serviced from the surplus on the 25,000 units above break-even.
4. Unit cost of $300,000 ÷ 75,000 + $8.00 = $12.00 can be benchmarked each quarter to spot the rework cost of the 2.4% defect rate and to negotiate the $8.00 variable cost with suppliers.

working_marks: 1 mark for the correct formula and 1 mark for the accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii); 1 mark per valid applied use in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate MGF's liquidity by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has MGF's liquidity improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.54 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.85 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.98 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 1.17 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $140,000 inventories + $190,000 trade receivables + $55,000 cash = $385,000; 2025 current assets = $165,000 + $210,000 + $70,000 = $445,000. The broader liquidity measure is $385,000 ÷ $250,000 = 1.54 in 2024 and $445,000 ÷ $240,000 = 1.85 in 2025. Excluding inventories, the stricter measure is ($385,000 − $140,000) ÷ $250,000 = $245,000 ÷ $250,000 = 0.98 in 2024 and ($445,000 − $165,000) ÷ $240,000 = $280,000 ÷ $240,000 = 1.17 in 2025.

Evaluation: Liquidity has strengthened on both measures. The broader measure rose from 1.54 to 1.85 because current liabilities fell from $250,000 to $240,000 while current assets grew by $60,000. More importantly, the stricter measure rose from 0.98 to 1.17, so MGF can now cover short-term debts without relying on selling inventories — valuable while it services a $450,000 loan and commits $720,000 to the CNC cell. The 2024 figure below 1.0 shows how thin the cash buffer was. However, trade receivables climbed from $190,000 to $210,000, tying up cash; if assemblers pay late, the improvement could reverse quickly. Inventories also rose to $165,000, and with a 2.4% defect rate some of that stock may be slow-moving.

Conclusion: MGF's liquidity has improved. Both measures are higher and the stricter one now exceeds 1.0, so the gain is not dependent on stock. The residual risk is rising receivables, so MGF should tighten credit control before drawing further on its loan.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States isolated financial figures or vague comments about liquidity with no accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Calculates the current ratio and acid test ratio for both years with some contextual comment on the trend for MGF.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years, detailed evaluation of inventories, receivables, cash and current liabilities, and a justified conclusion on whether MGF's liquidity improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for MGF of introducing a recycling scheme for steel offcuts from its CNC machining cell.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Recycling offcuts reduces the volume of waste sent to landfill and can lower material spending at a time when wholesale steel and alloy prices have risen 9.0%. Recovered scrap may be sold or re-melted, protecting the $6.00 contribution per unit on the 75,000 units MGF produces and helping fund the $720,000 machining cell without extra borrowing. It also supports the environmental standards expected by larger commercial vehicle assemblers.

Disadvantage: Segregating and storing different alloy grades needs bins, labour and a collection contract, adding to the $300,000 fixed-cost base before savings are certain. CNC swarf contaminated by cutting fluid may be worth little, so the scheme might not cover its own cost. With the defect rate already at 2.4% and $450,000 of loan interest to meet, management time spent on recycling could be better used reducing rework first. The scheme also competes for attention with the 11 of 60 skilled machinists who took unplanned leave and with the need to keep 75,000 units on schedule for commercial vehicle assemblers.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid point identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual explanation and analysis applied to MGF.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the base interest rate rise to 5.25%, the 7.2% minimum wage increase and the 9.0% rise in wholesale steel prices will affect MGF. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.50% to 5.25%): The increase is 0.75 percentage points. If the $450,000 ten-year loan carries a variable rate, the extra annual cost is 0.75% × $450,000 = $3,375 a year (0.0075 × $450,000). That is modest beside fixed costs of $300,000, and if the loan is fixed the direct effect is zero. Higher rates could still make future borrowing for the $720,000 cell more expensive.

Minimum wage increase (7.2%, from $12.50 to $13.40): Each paid hour rises by $13.40 − $12.50 = $0.90. MGF has a workforce of 60 and the insert gives no hours worked, so no annual wage total can be claimed honestly. The useful comparison is productivity: 75,000 units ÷ 60 workers = 1,250 units per worker. If that holds, the higher wage is absorbed by the $14.00 selling price; if absence among 11 of 60 machinists cuts output, unit labour cost rises. Agency cover at $280 a day makes absence expensive already.

Wholesale steel and alloy inflation (9.0%): The insert does not split the $8.00 variable cost into materials, so only an explicit bound is defensible. If the whole $8.00 were steel-linked, 9.0% × $8.00 = $0.72 a unit; across 75,000 units that is $72,000 a year (75,000 × $0.72). Even a quarter of that, $18,000, would cut into the $6.00 contribution on every part and compound the rework from the 2.4% defect rate.

Conclusion: The 9.0% rise in steel prices will have the greatest impact. It applies to every unit sold, cannot be avoided by fixing a loan rate, and directly erodes the contribution that justifies the $720,000 investment. The interest rise is small and conditional, while the wage rise can be offset if productivity stays at 1,250 units per worker.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the three external changes with limited application to MGF.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two of the external changes on MGF's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Evaluates all three external changes with explicit workings from insert figures and a justified judgement on which has the greatest impact on MGF.
